plot_extraction.response_text:
On New Year’s Eve, William obtains free sweets from Mr. Moss and, in return, agrees to make a resolution to be polite for New Year’s Day. Mr. Moss also reveals that he intends to repeat his annual marriage proposal to a woman who has refused him for ten years.

The next morning, William’s exaggerated politeness confuses and irritates his family. He then visits Mr. Moss, who asks him to watch the sweet shop briefly while he catches a train to make his proposal. When the replacement shopkeeper cannot come, William remains in charge and begins eating the stock.

Treating the shop as his own, William overcharges an unpleasant customer, gives a large quantity of sweets to a girl he admires, and invites his friends to help themselves. A confrontation with an older boy escalates into a street battle fought with acid drops, leaving the shop depleted and disordered.

Mr. Moss returns delighted because his proposal has finally been accepted. Too happy to care about the damage or lost stock, he thanks William for minding the shop. William abandons his resolution after half a day and heads home feeling sick from overeating sweets.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story uses a brisk, comic, omniscient narrative style associated with early twentieth-century children’s fiction. The narrator remains close to William’s point of view while retaining an amused adult perspective, presenting his appetites, fantasies, faulty reasoning and moral evasions with mock seriousness. William’s experiences are treated as momentous adventures, but the narration continually exposes the gap between his heroic self-image and the disorder he creates. Occasional direct addresses to the reader—most notably the rhetorical appeal near the ending—strengthen the confidential, storytelling tone.

The prose is clear, energetic and largely chronological. Short narrative passages alternate with extended stretches of rapid dialogue, giving scenes the timing of a stage comedy. Sentences are generally compact, although longer, more elaborately balanced sentences appear when the narrator comments ironically or heightens a comic description. Repetition is an important device: William repeatedly adds strained formulas such as “if you don’t mind me sayin’ so” to insults and lies, while phrases like “quite all right” acquire increasing comic force as circumstances become less and less all right. Lists and accumulations—especially the names of sweets and the catalogue of William’s depredations—create abundance, momentum and sensory excess.

Dialogue is the chief means of characterization. William’s speech is rendered phonetically through dropped consonants, contractions, non-standard grammar and childish mispronunciations: “goin’,” “wun’t,” “p’lite,” “menshun” and similar forms. Mr. Moss’s working-class pronunciation is represented in the same way, while the other characters’ speech varies according to age, temperament and social position. The thin customer speaks with rigid correctness and indignation; William’s family responds with suspicion, irony or teasing; his friends communicate in terse, excited phrases. This contrast between formal politeness and colloquial speech drives much of the humour.

The dominant tone is affectionate satire. William is greedy, dishonest, destructive and self-important, but he is not presented as malicious. His misconduct grows from literal-mindedness, impulsiveness and a limitless ability to believe his own inventions. The narrator describes these faults in elevated language, turning childish absurdity into mock epic: the resolution becomes “a kind of god,” the sweet-shop resembles “Aladdin’s Cave,” and the sweet-throwing brawl becomes a “noble fight against heavy odds.” Such mock-heroic phrasing comically dignifies trivial events while preserving sympathy for the protagonist.

Character description often depends on exaggerated contrast. William’s rough, freckled, noisy physicality is set against the little girl’s idealized white clothes, golden curls, blue eyes and “silvery” voice. His infatuation briefly shifts the prose into sentimental romantic parody, complete with melting emotion, imagined rescues and ceremonious generosity. The elevated language remains filtered through childish fantasy, however, and is punctured by physical comedy as William continues stuffing sweets into his mouth. Adults are likewise reduced to sharply defined comic types: the lugubrious shopkeeper, the suspicious father, the anxious mother and the censorious customer.

The humour arises primarily from incongruity, escalation and dramatic irony. William interprets politeness as a set of detachable verbal formulas rather than a mode of considerate behaviour, so courtesy is mechanically appended to rudeness, fraud and aggression. Each episode enlarges the consequences of this misunderstanding: a modest New Year’s resolution leads to shopkeeping, overeating, false pricing, reckless generosity, vandalism and street battle. Readers understand the likely consequences long before William does, while he repeatedly recasts accidents and unauthorized privileges as proof of his own importance.

The story’s structure is tightly comic and circular. It begins with William obtaining sweets through verbal ingenuity, establishes politeness as the central premise, then places him in a sweet-shop where appetite, fantasy and opportunity combine. A succession of visitors tests the premise in different ways: the messenger creates the practical crisis, the hostile customer exposes William’s dishonesty, the little girl prompts romantic generosity, his friends encourage excess, and the older boy triggers violence. The climax arrives with Mr. Moss’s return, but expected punishment is cancelled by the shopkeeper’s romantic happiness. The final consequence is therefore bodily rather than moral: William escapes blame but cannot escape nausea.

Sensory detail is concentrated around food. Brand-like names such as “Cokernut Kisses,” “Pineapple Crisp,” “Nutty Footballs” and “Mixed Dew Drops” give the shop a vivid, almost magical allure. Their playful capitalisation and extravagant variety recreate a child’s fascinated perception of confectionery. As consumption continues, the imagery shifts subtly from temptation to surfeit, culminating in William’s pallor, unsteadiness and aversion to lunch. This physical arc provides an understated comic punishment without imposing an explicit moral lesson.

Overall, the style combines colloquial immediacy, polished narrative irony, affectionate caricature and carefully controlled escalation. It views childhood neither sentimentally nor didactically, but as a self-contained world governed by appetite, imagination and ingenious misinterpretation. The closing mock-archaic phrase “I trow not” epitomizes the method: an adult narrator applies ceremonious language to a universal childhood catastrophe, ending the tale with sympathy, amusement and ironic grandeur.

generation.response_text:
### William’s Polite New Year

On the last afternoon of the old year William stood outside Mr. Moss’s sweet-shop with his hands in his pockets and his nose pressed thoughtfully against the window.

The window contained everything that a sweet-shop window ought to contain and a good many things that, in William’s opinion, no sweet-shop window had any right to contain unless it intended to give them to him. There were glass jars of Cokernut Kisses, Pineapple Crisp, Rose Rock, Nutty Footballs, Lemon Fizzers, Chocolate Soldiers, Almond Cannons and Mixed Dew Drops. There were slabs of toffee as large as paving-stones. There were striped sticks of peppermint, long and stout and serviceable enough to support a tent. There were sugar mice with pink eyes and liquorice tails. There were chocolate cigars, which William regarded with the tolerant contempt of one who had once eaten six and been unable to look at a real cigar box for a week.

Mr. Moss, behind the counter, watched him mournfully.

Mr. Moss always looked mournful. When business was good he looked mournful because the stock was going; when business was bad he looked mournful because it was not. His black moustache drooped over his mouth, and his shoulders drooped over his waistcoat, and his waistcoat drooped over his trousers. He had the appearance of having received, many years ago, news too depressing ever to be contradicted.

William entered.

“Afternoon,” he said.

“Afternoon,” said Mr. Moss.

William looked round the shop with the air of a wealthy customer who is disappointed by the limited selection.

“How much are those?” he said, pointing at a jar.

“Penny an ounce.”

“I’ve only got a halfpenny.”

“Then you can’t ’ave an ounce.”

“I didn’t say I wanted an ounce,” said William with dignity. “I only asked how much it was.”

There was silence. William transferred his attention to the Pineapple Crisp.

“How much is that?”

“Penny an ounce.”

“An’ those?”

“Penny an ounce.”

“Are they all a penny an ounce?”

“Most of ’em.”

“It’s funny,” said William, “all of ’em bein’ the same price. Seems sort of not fair to the ones that are nicer.”

Mr. Moss sighed.

William took his halfpenny from his pocket and placed it on the counter. It was not a handsome halfpenny. Indeed, it had spent so long in William’s possession that it had acquired the appearance of sharing his habits and fortunes.

“What can I have for that?” he asked.

“’Alf an ounce of anything that’s a penny.”

William considered this. Half an ounce was a contemptible quantity. It was the sort of quantity one might give to a canary.

“It’s New Year’s Eve,” he said at last.

Mr. Moss admitted it.

“People give presents on New Year’s Eve,” pursued William.

“Do they?”

“Yes. Everyone knows that.”

“Who gives ’em?”

“People,” said William comprehensively.

Mr. Moss looked at him. William looked back, grave, patient and full of information.

“Well, no one’s given me any,” said Mr. Moss.

“I would,” said William warmly, “if I had any money.”

“You’ve got an ’alfpenny.”

“That’s all the money I’ve got,” explained William. “I couldn’t give you that, ’cause then I wouldn’t have any.”

Mr. Moss sighed again and reached for the jar of Mixed Dew Drops.

“’Alf an ounce,” he said.

William watched the scales with an expression of anguish.

“A bit fell off,” he pointed out.

Mr. Moss put back the fragment that had fallen from the scoop.

“I meant it fell off on to your side,” said William.

Mr. Moss put it in the bag.

“An’ that little blue one’s not quite on the scale.”

Mr. Moss added the little blue one.

“An’ that red one was sort of touching it before you moved it.”

Mr. Moss added the red one.

By the time William’s scientific observations were complete, the bag contained nearly two ounces.

Mr. Moss twisted the paper at the top.

“Now,” he said, “you make a New Year resolution.”

William regarded him suspiciously.

“What sort?”

“Resolve to be a good boy.”

“I am a good boy.”

Mr. Moss’s moustache moved slightly.

“Well, resolve to be better.”

“Better than who?”

“Better than you are now.”

William considered the proposition. It seemed to him unnecessary and faintly insulting.

“I’ll resolve not to do somethin’,” he offered.

“Resolve to be polite,” said Mr. Moss. “Just for one day. Tomorrow. New Year’s Day.”

William frowned. Politeness was, in his experience, a tiresome arrangement by which adults delayed saying what they meant. Still, he had his eyes on the paper bag.

“If I do, d’you give me these free?”

“I’ll give you those free.”

“An’ my halfpenny back?”

Mr. Moss pushed the halfpenny towards him.

“All right,” said William. “I resolve to be p’lite all tomorrow.”

“Properly polite.”

“Yes.”

“Not just when it suits you.”

William was shocked.

“A resolution’s a resolution,” he said. “I never break resolutions.”

This was true, chiefly because he had never before made one.

He took the sweets and put three into his mouth.

“Are you makin’ one?” he asked indistinctly.

Mr. Moss’s expression became, if possible, more lugubrious.

“I make the same one every year.”

“What?”

“To ask Miss Marjorie Bell to marry me.”

“Does she?”

“Does she what?”

“Marry you?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“She says no.”

“Why d’you keep on askin’ her, then?”

Mr. Moss looked beyond William at the darkening street.

“I’ve asked her every New Year’s Day for ten years,” he said. “She expects it.”

“P’raps she says no ’cause she expects that too.”

Mr. Moss stared at him.

William, encouraged, went on.

“You ought to do somethin’ diff’rent. Say you don’t want to marry her. Then she might say she does.”

“Go ’ome,” said Mr. Moss.

William moved towards the door.

“I don’t think she sounds very sensible,” he said, “if you don’t mind me sayin’ so.”

“Go ’ome.”

William went home, finishing the Mixed Dew Drops on the way.

That night he contemplated his resolution. He contemplated it in bed, when he should have been asleep, and clothed it in splendour. He saw himself moving among his family like a courtier of ancient days, bowing, smiling, yielding the largest chair and the last potato. His mother would weep with pride. His father would gaze upon him in silent wonder. His brother and sister, humbled by his example, would confess that they had misjudged him. Possibly there would be a medal.

The resolution ceased to be merely a promise made for sweets. It became a stern and shining law. It hovered above him like a kind of god, demanding sacrifice.

At eight o’clock the next morning William entered the dining-room.

His family were at breakfast.

“Good mornin’, Father,” he said. “I hope you’ve slept well, if you don’t mind me sayin’ so.”

His father lowered the newspaper.

“What?”

“I said I hope you’ve slept well.”

“Why?”

William was taken aback.

“’Cause it’s p’lite.”

His elder brother Robert looked at him with deep suspicion.

“What have you done?”

“Nothin’.”

“What are you going to do?”

“Nothin’.”

His mother turned anxiously from the coffee-pot.

“Are you feeling quite well, dear?”

“Yes, thank you very much, Mother, if you don’t mind me sayin’ so.”

His sister Ethel stared at him.

“That doesn’t make sense.”

“It does,” said William. Then he remembered. “It does, thank you very much, if you don’t mind me sayin’ so.”

He sat down and took the toast-rack.

“Pass that,” said Robert.

William drew himself up.

“Would you mind sayin’ ‘please’?”

Robert blinked.

“Pass the toast.”

“Not unless you say ‘please.’ It isn’t p’lite.”

“Give it to me.”

“I’m only tryin’ to improve your manners, if you don’t mind me sayin’ so.”

Robert reached across the table. William snatched the toast-rack away. In the brief struggle that followed, two pieces of toast fell into the marmalade and one into Father’s coffee.

Father rose.

“William!”

William hastily surrendered the toast-rack.

“Here you are,” he said graciously. “Quite all right. Don’t menshun it.”

“Don’t mention what?”

“Me givin’ it to him.”

“You didn’t give it to him. You upset my coffee.”

“I’m sorry you put your coffee where the toast fell into it, if you don’t mind me sayin’ so.”

“Go and wash your hands.”

“They’re clean.”

“They’re filthy.”

William examined them.

“They’re cleaner than Robert’s, if you don’t mind me sayin’ so.”

“Go.”

William retired with dignity. He felt that politeness, properly practised, was a noble but lonely calling.

He returned and seated himself again.

“May I have an egg, please?” he said.

His mother brightened.

“Of course, dear.”

William took two.

“Only one,” she said.

“I said ‘please.’”

“That doesn’t mean you may have two.”

William slowly replaced the smaller egg.

“Thank you very much for lettin’ me have the bigger one.”

“I didn’t.”

“Well, you didn’t say I couldn’t, if you don’t mind me sayin’ so.”

His father laid down the newspaper.

“William, if this extraordinary behaviour is intended to annoy us—”

“It isn’t. I made a resolution.”

“A resolution?”

“To be p’lite all day.”

Robert laughed.

“I thought something had happened to him.”

“I am bein’ p’lite,” said William fiercely, “which is more than what you are, if you don’t mind me sayin’ so.”

“William,” said his mother, “politeness does not consist of saying ‘if you don’t mind me saying so’ after every rude remark.”

“What does it consist of, then?”

“Thinking of other people.”

William looked bewildered. This was an entirely new and unreasonable definition.

“You can’t tell whether anyone’s doin’ that,” he objected.

“You can generally tell.”

“Well, I’m thinkin’ of everyone now.”

“What are you thinking?”

“I’m thinkin’ Father looks cross an’ Robert’s hair wants cuttin’ an’ Ethel’s got marmalade on her chin, if you don’t mind me sayin’ so.”

Breakfast ended abruptly.

At ten o’clock William went out.

He went first to Mr. Moss’s shop, partly to display the success of the resolution and partly because there was always the possibility that Mr. Moss might celebrate it with more sweets.

Mr. Moss stood behind the counter in a black coat, a high collar and a bright green tie. The tie had evidently been chosen to suggest hope, though on Mr. Moss it suggested chiefly sea-sickness.

“Mornin’,” said William. “You look very nice, if you don’t mind me sayin’ so.”

Mr. Moss adjusted the tie.

“Do I?”

“Yes. Except the green doesn’t suit you much.”

Mr. Moss sighed.

“I’m catchin’ the ten-forty train,” he said. “I’m goin’ to see Miss Bell.”

“To ask her again?”

“Yes.”

“She’ll prob’ly say no again,” said William. “Still, you look very nice.”

Mr. Moss took out his watch.

“Mrs. Cripps is comin’ to mind the shop while I’m gone. She should be ’ere now.”

At that moment a small boy entered carrying a note. Mr. Moss opened it.

“Mrs. Cripps’s got lumbago,” he read. “She can’t come.”

“What’s lumbago?” said William.

“Pain in the back.”

“I had a pain in my back once. I still went to school.”

Mr. Moss looked at the clock, at the note and at William.

“You couldn’t stay ’ere ten minutes, could you? Just till I find someone?”

William’s eyes widened.

“Mind the shop?”

“Yes. Don’t touch anything. If a customer comes, tell ’em to wait.”

William drew himself to his full height.

“I’ll look after everythin’,” he said. “You can trust me.”

Mr. Moss hesitated. Then the station clock struck the quarter.

“I’ll miss that train,” he muttered. “Mrs. Brown next door might come in when she’s finished upstairs. I’ll send word. Don’t sell anything. Don’t give anything away. Don’t eat anything.”

“I know how to keep a shop,” said William with cold dignity.

Mr. Moss seized his hat.

“I wun’t be more’n two hours if—if it’s the usual answer.”

“It will be,” said William encouragingly.

Mr. Moss hurried out.

William was alone.

For a moment he stood behind the counter, motionless, conscious of responsibility. The shop was entrusted to him. Its wealth lay all around him. He was master of an Aladdin’s Cave whose treasures surpassed mere jewels, because no one could eat jewels with pleasure.

He surveyed the jars.

Of course he had been told not to touch anything. But the command had plainly been intended for an ordinary boy. A shopkeeper, on the other hand, had to test his stock. It would be dishonest to sell stale sweets.

He removed one Cokernut Kiss and ate it.

It was fresh.

He tested a Pineapple Crisp. That also was fresh.

The Nutty Footballs presented a difficulty. One might be fresh while another was stale. He tested three.

Then he remembered his resolution. It was New Year’s Day, and he had undertaken to be polite. It was surely impolite to accept Mr. Moss’s hospitality grudgingly. He ate a Chocolate Soldier out of gratitude.

The door-bell rang.

A thin woman entered. She had a long nose, a stiff hat and a shopping-bag which she placed upon the counter as though bringing evidence before a court.

“Where is Mr. Moss?” she demanded.

“He’s out.”

“Who are you?”

“I’m mindin’ the shop.”

“You?”

“Yes, thank you very much.”

The thin woman looked him over.

“I wish to purchase two ounces of violet creams.”

William found the jar.

“How much are they?” she asked.

He had no idea. He looked at the label, but the price was written in Mr. Moss’s private hand, which resembled a line of ants after an accident.

“Sixpence an ounce,” he said.

The woman gave a cry.

“Nonsense! I bought them yesterday at threepence.”

“They’ve gone up.”

“Since yesterday?”

“Yes. New Year prices.”

“There is no such thing.”

“There is here.”

“I shall not pay it.”

“Quite all right,” said William. “You don’t have to have ’em.”

The woman stiffened.

“I have always had two ounces of violet creams on New Year’s Day.”

“Well, you can have ’em now. They’re only sixpence an ounce.”

“They are marked threepence.”

William leaned over the label.

“That says sixpence.”

“It distinctly says threepence.”

“It’s upside down,” said William.

The woman turned the jar round.

“Now it says threepence.”

“Yes, but now it’s the wrong way round.”

“This is outrageous.”

William remembered his resolution.

“You’re a very disagreeable woman, if you don’t mind me sayin’ so.”

The thin woman opened her mouth. No sound came from it at first.

“I shall report you to Mr. Moss.”

“Quite all right. Don’t menshun it.”

She swept out, leaving her shopping-bag behind. William placed it under the counter. He did not call her back because, after all, she had been disagreeable.

He ate another Pineapple Crisp to restore himself.

The bell rang again.

A little girl entered.

She wore a white coat with white fur at the neck, white stockings and shining black shoes. Golden curls escaped from beneath a white woollen cap. Her eyes were blue. Her voice, when she spoke, was silvery.

William, who had been attempting to put an entire Nutty Football into his mouth, removed it hurriedly.

“Please,” she said, “may I have a pennyworth of lemon drops?”

William gazed at her.

In one instant he became a different being. He was no longer William, temporary custodian of a sweet-shop with crumbs on his jersey. He was a prince, a knight, a rescuer of maidens from burning castles and swollen rivers. He saw himself carrying the little girl through flames, fighting wolves on a mountainside, and returning her lost white kitten while trumpets sounded.

“What’s your name?” he asked.

“Lucinda.”

William had never heard a more beautiful name.

“I’m William.”

She waited.

“Do you own this shop?”

William hesitated for only a fraction of a second.

“I’m runnin’ it.”

“Oh.”

“You can have anythin’ you like.”

“I only have a penny.”

“You don’t need money,” said William magnificently. “Not here.”

He took a large paper bag and began to fill it. Lemon drops went in first, then Cokernut Kisses, Rose Rock, Chocolate Soldiers, Mixed Dew Drops, peppermint sticks and several sugar mice.

Lucinda watched anxiously.

“I don’t think Mummy would like me to have so many.”

“They’re good for you.”

“Mummy says sweets are bad for teeth.”

“Only cheap sweets,” explained William. “These are special ones. They make teeth stronger.”

He added a slab of toffee.

“Will they really?”

“Yes. They’re what dentists eat.”

Lucinda accepted the bag.

“Thank you very much.”

William flushed beneath his freckles.

“Quite all right,” he murmured. “Don’t menshun it.”

She smiled at him and went out.

For a long moment William stood entranced. Then he put the rejected Nutty Football back into his mouth and resumed the duties of commerce.

Mrs. Brown did not come.

Eleven o’clock passed, then half-past eleven. William began to feel that he had always kept a shop and always would. He arranged three jars according to colour, sampled the Almond Cannons, and made a notice:

NEW YEAR SALE  
EVERYTHINK CHEEP  
SOME THINGS FREE TO PEOPLE I LIKE

He placed it in the window.

Soon Ted and Peter appeared. They had been wandering about in search of William and were arrested by the sight of him behind the counter.

“Who gave you the shop?” said Ted.

“Mr. Moss.”

“What for?”

“’Cause he trusts me.”

“Can you eat the sweets?”

“Course. Shopkeepers always eat their own sweets.”

Peter entered cautiously.

“Won’t he mind?”

“No. I’m helpin’ him. He said to look after everythin’.”

“What can we have?”

William waved his hand.

“Anything you want, if you don’t mind me sayin’ so.”

Ted seized the Cokernut Kisses. Peter chose Chocolate Soldiers. Sam, arriving a few minutes later, devoted himself to Acid Drops. The shop became filled with the sounds of paper bags crackling, jar lids knocking and jaws working.

They played at shopkeeping.

Ted came in as a duke and bought ten pounds of liquorice bootlaces to feed his racehorses. Peter was an explorer fitting out an expedition with peppermint sticks. Sam became a pirate and stole the till, which, fortunately, contained only fourpence and a tram ticket.

William, as proprietor, served them all with pomp.

“Certainly, sir.”

“Thank you very much, sir.”

“Quite all right, sir.”

“You’re a fat-headed idiot, sir, if you don’t mind me sayin’ so.”

It was while Peter was trying to balance a sugar mouse on the end of his nose that Hubert Lane entered.

Hubert was fourteen, large, smooth-haired and unpleasant. He lived in the next road and considered it his duty to remind all smaller boys of his age and size. Behind him stood two companions of corresponding character, though lesser magnificence.

“What’s going on?” Hubert said.

“Nothin’,” said William.

“You’ve been giving away Moss’s sweets.”

“No, I haven’t.”

Hubert pointed to Ted’s bulging pockets.

“He bought ’em.”

“How much?”

“A pound.”

Ted nodded earnestly.

“I paid a pound.”

“You haven’t got a pound.”

“I’m goin’ to pay him later.”

Hubert smiled.

“I’m going to tell Moss.”

William came round the counter.

“You’d better not.”

“Who’ll stop me?”

“Me.”

Hubert laughed.

William’s resolution stirred faintly within him.

“You’re a sneak, if you don’t mind me sayin’ so.”

“And you’re a thief.”

“I’m not. Mr. Moss put me in charge.”

“So you ate everything?”

“We had to test it.”

Hubert picked up an Acid Drop and put it into his mouth.

“Put that back,” ordered William.

Hubert sucked it thoughtfully.

“Put it back.”

“All right.”

He removed the sweet from his mouth and held it out.

William recoiled.

“I don’t want it now.”

“You told me to put it back.”

Hubert dropped it into the jar.

There are moments when diplomacy ceases to be a virtue. William knew this instinctively. He seized the Acid Drop, now possessing qualities beyond those intended by its manufacturer, and threw it at Hubert.

It struck Hubert on the cheek.

Hubert seized a handful from the jar and flung them.

The battle began.

At first it was confined to the shop. William, Ted, Peter and Sam took cover behind the counter and replied with Lemon Fizzers. Hubert and his allies overturned a display-box and bombarded them with Nutty Footballs. A jar of Mixed Dew Drops fell, rolled across the floor and opened beneath the feet of the combatants. The effect was immediate and spectacular.

Hubert slid into a chair. Peter sat down suddenly in a box of toffee. Ted, attempting to retreat, caught his foot in the thin woman’s shopping-bag and brought down a festoon of peppermint sticks.

William fought on.

He stood behind the weighing-machine, hair wild, face scarlet, eyes blazing, hurling Acid Drops with the grave concentration of an artillery officer defending the last fortress of civilization.

“Give in!” shouted Hubert.

“Never!”

A Pineapple Crisp struck William on the forehead. He responded with a Chocolate Soldier at close range.

Hubert retreated into the street.

William followed.

So did the others.

The battle spread along the pavement. Passers-by stopped. A small dog ate enthusiastically from the gutter. Two little boys joined William’s side without understanding the cause. A delivery boy joined Hubert’s because Hubert promised him a packet of liquorice.

The air was thick with confectionery.

Acid Drops rattled against windows. Cokernut Kisses burst whitely on the road. Sugar mice flew through space with their liquorice tails streaming behind them. Rose Rock shattered upon the kerb. A peppermint stick struck a lamp-post and broke in half with the clean, noble sound of a sword.

William fought a noble fight against heavy odds. At least, that was how he saw it. He did not see a small freckled boy, sticky from head to foot, using another man’s stock to pelt three older boys. He saw a leader rallying his faithful band while enemies closed in on every side.

“More ammunition!” he cried.

Ted ran into the shop and returned with Almond Cannons.

They charged.

Hubert’s forces wavered. One Almond Cannon entered Hubert’s collar. Another struck his companion on the nose. The delivery boy deserted.

At that moment a figure appeared at the end of the street.

It was Mr. Moss.

William saw him and stopped.

The battle stopped.

Hubert Lane, remembering an appointment elsewhere, disappeared with his friends. Ted, Peter and Sam melted into the alley beside the butcher’s shop. The two little boys went on eating from the gutter as though they had never taken part in warfare.

William stood alone before the wrecked shop.

The window display had collapsed. The floor was carpeted with broken sweets, paper bags and fragments of glass. A long pink ribbon of toffee hung from the door handle. One jar lay on its side in the road. The notice in the window now read:

NEW YEAR  
EVERYTHINK  
FREE

Mr. Moss approached.

He wore no hat. His green tie had risen over one shoulder. His moustache still drooped, but behind it was a smile so vast and radiant that it transformed his whole mournful person.

“She said yes!” he shouted.

William stared.

“She said yes, William! After ten years, she said yes!”

He seized William’s hand and shook it.

“Well,” said William faintly, “that’s good.”

“I missed the ten-forty. Had to catch the eleven-fifteen. Thought I’d missed ’er. Found ’er at the station. I said, ‘Marjorie, will you marry me?’ She said, ‘Yes, Alfred, I think I’d better.’ Just like that!”

He laughed aloud. It was an extraordinary sound from Mr. Moss. Several people turned to look.

Then he saw the shop.

He looked at the broken window display, the overturned jars, the Acid Drops in the road, the toffee on the door handle and William’s sugar-coated hair.

William drew breath.

“There was a customer,” he began, “an’ she was very rude, if you don’t mind me sayin’ so, an’ then a girl came an’ you’d’ve wanted me to give her some things, an’ then Ted and Peter only had a few, an’ Hubert stole an Acid Drop, an’ when I told him p’litely to put it back he did, but it was wet, an’ then he started the fight—”

Mr. Moss laughed again.

“Quite all right,” he said.

William stopped.

“What?”

“Quite all right. Don’t matter. Nothin’ matters today.”

He looked round his ruined kingdom with the benevolent indifference of an emperor who has just acquired another continent.

“Stock was insured,” he said vaguely. “Some of it. P’raps. Never mind. She said yes.”

He patted William on the shoulder.

“Thank you for mindin’ the shop.”

William swallowed.

“Quite all right,” he said. “Don’t menshun it.”

Mr. Moss entered the shop, still smiling.

William walked away.

At the corner he met Ted, Peter and Sam.

“What did he do?” whispered Ted.

“Nothin’.”

“Didn’t he hit you?”

“No.”

“Didn’t he say he’d tell your father?”

“No. He thanked me.”

The three looked at William with admiration. His mysterious influence over adults had long been acknowledged, but this exceeded even their expectations.

“What shall we do now?” said Peter.

William leaned against the wall. The street moved gently beneath him. His face had become pale beneath the freckles. Within him Cokernut Kisses, Pineapple Crisp, Nutty Footballs, Chocolate Soldiers, Almond Cannons, Rose Rock and Mixed Dew Drops seemed to be holding a battle of their own, conducted without discipline and in total darkness.

“I’m goin’ home,” he said.

“What about your polite resolution?” asked Sam.

William considered it.

Politeness had brought him suspicion at breakfast, an argument with a customer, an acquaintance with Lucinda, command of a sweet-shop, a battle with Hubert Lane and the complete destruction of Mr. Moss’s stock. It had had a fair trial.

“I’ve done it half a day,” he said. “Half a day’s enough for a whole year.”

He set off homeward with slow and careful steps.

At lunch his mother looked at him anxiously.

“You’re very pale, dear. Aren’t you hungry?”

“No.”

“Would you like some roast beef?”

William shuddered.

“Potatoes?”

He closed his eyes.

“Treacle pudding?”

William rose abruptly and left the room.

His father watched the door close.

“I knew that politeness meant trouble,” he said.

And perhaps William had been greedy, dishonest, reckless and destructive. Perhaps his courtesy had been no more than a string of phrases tied, like bright labels, to conduct of quite another kind. But had he not kept a lonely shop, served the public, encouraged friendship, defended property, rewarded beauty and assisted—however indirectly—at the happy ending of a ten-year courtship?

Could any reasonable person demand more of a New Year’s resolution?

I think not.

## The Map of Small Departures

Every morning at six, before the first train rattled over the eastern bridge, Clara Vale unlocked the doors of the Lost Property Office.

The office occupied a narrow room beneath Platform Nine, where the walls trembled whenever an express arrived. It had no windows, only a row of yellow lamps and shelves that rose from floor to ceiling. On those shelves rested the forgotten things of the city: umbrellas, gloves, hats, books, spectacles, suitcases, walking sticks, toys, tools, wedding rings, and once, memorably, a wooden leg.

Clara had worked there for twenty-seven years.

She knew that people imagined lost property as a kingdom of accidents. A scarf slipped from a shoulder. A wallet left on a bench. A parcel abandoned in a rush. But after so many years, Clara believed that forgetting was rarely simple. People left things behind for reasons they could not explain, and the objects arrived beneath Platform Nine carrying the silence of those reasons.

There was the violin with a broken E string, never claimed. The leather suitcase containing six identical white shirts and a photograph torn neatly in half. The child’s red boot, its sole still crusted with seaside sand though the nearest shore lay a hundred miles away.

Clara catalogued each item in precise blue handwriting.

**Item 4,821: One green umbrella, silver handle, small tear near edge. Found on northbound service.**

**Item 4,822: One brass key, tied with black thread. Found beneath seat, carriage three.**

**Item 4,823: One paper map, hand-drawn, no place names. Found in station waiting room.**

The map arrived on a Tuesday in November.

A porter named Ellis brought it down just before noon. Rain glittered on the shoulders of his uniform.

“Probably rubbish,” he said, placing a folded sheet of paper on Clara’s desk. “But it looked deliberate.”

Everything looked deliberate to Clara. She unfolded it carefully.

It was a map of the city, or appeared to be. The river curved through the center, crossed by seven bridges. The railway station was drawn as a black rectangle. Streets branched outward in gray pencil, though none were labeled.

Instead, the mapmaker had marked certain locations with tiny blue crosses.

There were dozens of them.

Beside each cross was a brief note.

**Where I first lied to my mother.**

**Where the dog waited after the butcher died.**

**Where someone sang at 3:17 in the morning.**

**Where I decided not to leave.**

The handwriting was small and severe.

Ellis leaned over the desk. “Recognize any of it?”

Clara did not answer at once. Near the river, beside the shape of a public garden, one blue cross bore the words:

**Where Clara Vale buried the silver button.**

Her hand moved instinctively to the collar of her blouse.

“Miss Vale?”

“No,” she said. “I don’t recognize it.”

She folded the map, entered it in the ledger, and placed it in Drawer C beneath a collection of passports.

For the rest of the day, she made three mistakes.

She wrote *blue* instead of *black*. She assigned the same number to two different umbrellas. At closing time, she left the office without locking the inner cabinet, something she had not done once in twenty-seven years.

The silver button had belonged to her brother Daniel.

He had been eleven when he gave it to her, and Clara nine. They were playing in the public garden on the far side of the river, in the shadow of an iron statue of a forgotten general. Daniel had torn the button from his coat and pressed it into her palm.

“Treasure,” he had said.

“What makes it treasure?”

“We’re the only ones who know where it is.”

They buried it beneath a rosebush using a spoon stolen from their mother’s kitchen.

Three years later, Daniel disappeared.

He left for school one gray morning and never arrived. The police searched alleys, canals, empty houses, and railway yards. Clara’s father put up notices until the city seemed wallpapered with Daniel’s face. Her mother waited by the front window every evening for eighteen years.

No trace was ever found.

Clara had told no one about the button. Not her parents. Not the police. Not even her husband, during the seven quiet years before illness took him. It had become a private room in her memory, locked and undisturbed.

Yet someone had drawn it on a map.

The next morning, Clara opened Drawer C before removing her coat.

The map was still there.

She carried it to her desk and examined every mark. Some referred to ordinary events, others to things impossible for a stranger to know.

**Where Mr. Alton dropped the watch he stole.**

**Where two sisters exchanged names.**

**Where the yellow house used to stand.**

Then, at the northern edge of the city, Clara saw a note that stopped her breath.

**Where Daniel Vale waited for six days.**

The cross lay beside an abandoned branch of the railway, beyond the old glassworks.

Clara stared until the pencil lines blurred.

At nine, a young man came to claim a black suitcase. At ten, a woman asked about a pearl earring. At half past eleven, Ellis brought down a wet overcoat and a box containing a pigeon.

Clara performed her duties automatically. All the while, the map lay beneath her ledger.

At noon, she put on her coat.

She had taken only eight days of leave in twenty-seven years. Four for her husband’s funeral, three for her mother’s, and one when a burst pipe flooded her bedroom. Walking out in the middle of a shift felt like stepping from a moving train.

Ellis was on the platform.

“I need you to watch the office,” she told him.

“Is something wrong?”

“Yes,” Clara said, surprising herself with the truth. “I think it may have been wrong for a long time.”

Outside, rain had polished the city. She crossed the station square and boarded a northbound tram.

The old glassworks stood in a district the city had forgotten. Its chimneys had been demolished, its windows bricked over. Weeds split the pavement. Clara followed the map past warehouses and beneath a rusted railway arch.

There, hidden behind a wall of elder bushes, she found a narrow building made of soot-darkened brick.

It had once been a signalman’s cottage. The roof sagged. Most of the windows were broken.

The blue cross marked its back room.

Clara entered through a door hanging from one hinge. Inside, rain tapped through holes in the ceiling. The floor was littered with plaster, leaves, bottles, and the remains of a fire.

She imagined Daniel at twelve years old, sitting beside that fire. Waiting.

For whom?

For six days.

On the wall, almost concealed beneath peeling wallpaper, someone had scratched a line of words:

**I did not know the way home.**

Clara touched the letters.

“Daniel?”

Only the rain answered.

She searched the room. In a corner stood a collapsed cupboard. Behind it, she found a tin biscuit box. The lid had rusted shut, but she pried it open with a strip of metal.

Inside were three marbles, a pencil stub, two train tickets dated forty-eight years earlier, and a silver button.

Clara sat down on the floor.

The button was tarnished, but she recognized the small anchor engraved on its face. Daniel’s winter coat had been fastened with six of them.

It could not be the same button they had buried. The garden lay miles away.

Her fingers closed around it.

Beneath the button was a folded note.

**Clara,**

**I went back for the treasure. I thought you would understand. I saw the man watching our house again, so I came here like Father said. He said if anything bad happened, I should wait by the old signal line. I have waited six days. I cannot go home because the man may follow me. I am taking the morning freight west. I will send for you when it is safe.**

**I am sorry.**

**D.**

Clara read the note twice, then a third time.

Their father had known.

The thought rearranged the past with terrible speed.

She remembered whispers behind closed doors. Men in dark coats. Her father burning papers in the kitchen stove. The year before Daniel vanished, he had worked as an accountant for the glassworks. The factory closed after its owner was arrested for fraud, but the case had collapsed when important records disappeared.

Her father had died when Clara was twenty. A fall, they said, from the eastern bridge.

Perhaps Daniel had seen something. Perhaps he had been hidden. Perhaps their father, out of fear or shame, had allowed the family to believe the worst.

Clara unfolded the map again. A thin pencil line ran west from the cottage to the old freight route. She had mistaken it for a road.

Along the line were three more crosses.

**Where Daniel stole bread.**

**Where Daniel slept beneath the blue wagon.**

**Where Daniel was given another name.**

The final cross lay beyond the city’s edge.

Clara returned to the station near dusk. Ellis had organized the day’s arrivals into careful rows but had entered nothing in the ledger.

“I didn’t want to spoil your system,” he said.

Clara placed the biscuit tin on her desk.

“Who found the map?”

Ellis frowned. “An old gentleman in the waiting room.”

“What did he look like?”

“Tall. Gray coat. Gloves. He left before I could ask anything.”

“Did he board a train?”

“I don’t know.” Ellis paused. “He asked if you still worked here.”

Clara gripped the desk.

“And you did not think that worth mentioning?”

“People ask for you all the time.”

“No one asks for me.”

“They do,” Ellis said. “You just never notice.”

She almost laughed, though the sound that escaped her was closer to a sob.

The final cross on the map was labeled only:

**Where Daniel Vale became Thomas Gray.**

Beneath it, in smaller writing:

**House with three pears.**

Clara requested leave for the following day. Her supervisor, too astonished to object, granted her a week.

At sunrise, she took the western train.

As the city thinned into fields, Clara sat beside the window with the map on her lap. The final mark lay near a village called Bellweather, two hours away.

During the journey, doubt traveled with her.

The note might be false. The button could have been copied. Someone might be playing a cruel, elaborate trick.

And if Daniel had survived, why had he never returned?

Forty-eight years was not an accident. It was a life.

The train stopped at Bellweather shortly after ten. The village consisted of a church, a post office, a bakery, and rows of pale houses pressed between green hills.

Clara asked the woman in the post office if she knew a man named Thomas Gray.

“Which one?” the woman said. “Old Thomas or his son?”

“Old Thomas.”

“You’ll find him at the orchard, if he’s well enough. Follow the lane past the church.”

The orchard stood behind a low stone wall. Most of the trees were bare, their branches black against the white sky.

Near the gate, three pears had been painted on a wooden sign.

Clara stopped.

A man was repairing a fence inside the orchard. He wore a brown coat and leaned heavily on a cane. His hair was silver.

“Mr. Gray?” she called.

He straightened slowly.

Clara had prepared questions during the journey. She had arranged them with the same precision she used for unclaimed luggage.

Who made the map?

Why did you leave?

Why did Father lie?

Why did you not come back?

But when the man turned, every question vanished.

Age had altered him, but not completely. His left ear still stood out farther than his right. A pale line crossed his eyebrow where Clara had struck him with a wooden sword when they were children.

He looked at her for a long time.

Then he said, “You kept your hair short.”

His voice was older, roughened, but it was his.

Clara opened the gate.

She crossed the grass and struck him across the face.

The sound startled birds from the nearest pear tree.

Daniel touched his cheek.

“That,” Clara said, “was for Mother.”

He nodded.

She struck him again.

“That was for me.”

“I know.”

“No,” she said. “You do not.”

He lowered his hand. “No. I suppose I don’t.”

Clara wanted to hit him a third time, but instead she seized the front of his coat and held on as if he might disappear again. For a moment neither of them moved.

Then Daniel put his arms around her.

She had imagined this embrace as a child, as a young woman, and even, secretly, as an old one. In her imagination, it had always restored everything. Their mother rose from the grave. Their father’s lies dissolved. The empty years folded shut.

But the embrace restored nothing.

It was awkward, painful, and forty-eight years late.

Clara wept against his shoulder anyway.

They went to the house, where Daniel made tea. He moved carefully, apologizing whenever a spoon or cup made too much noise.

On the mantel stood photographs. Daniel beside a dark-haired woman. Daniel holding two infants. Daniel with a boy on his shoulders. Daniel at a wedding, at a lake, beneath a pear tree bright with spring blossom.

A whole life in silver frames.

“My wife, Ruth,” he said. “She died three years ago. We had two sons. One lives north, the other abroad.”

“Did they know?”

“Not until recently.”

“Did your wife?”

“Yes.”

“But not your mother.”

He closed his eyes.

Clara set down her cup. “Explain.”

Daniel told her.

Their father had uncovered records proving that the glassworks owner had bribed officials and arranged the death of an employee who threatened to speak. When Daniel saw one of the owner’s men watching their house, their father gave him instructions: if danger came, go to the signalman’s cottage and wait.

A man followed Daniel on his way to school. Frightened, Daniel ran to the cottage. Their father never came.

After six days, Daniel boarded a freight train. He fell ill in Bellweather and was found by a widow named Margaret Gray, who cared for him. When he recovered, he wrote home.

His letter was returned unopened.

Months later, he received a message from their father.

“Father found you?” Clara asked.

Daniel nodded. “He said the men were still watching. He said if I returned, I would put you and Mother in danger. He brought papers with a new name. He promised it would only be for a year or two.”

“But it wasn’t.”

“No.”

“Why?”

“At first, fear. Then shame. The longer I waited, the harder returning became. Father wrote that you were safe. Later he wrote that Mother believed I was dead and that telling her otherwise might destroy her.”

“He lied.”

“Yes.”

“And after he died?”

“I didn’t know he had. His letters stopped. I thought he wanted nothing more to do with me.”

“You could have come.”

“I could have.”

The simplicity of the answer made Clara hate him more than any excuse would have.

“Mother waited by the window every night.”

Daniel bowed his head.

“She would not let us move,” Clara continued. “She said you would not know where to find us. Every birthday she baked the cake you liked. Chocolate with walnuts. She did that until she could no longer stand.”

“I’m sorry.”

“Sorry is a word people use when they have nothing large enough to offer.”

“I know.”

“Stop saying that.”

He looked up. Tears stood in his eyes.

Clara turned toward the photographs. She studied the faces of nephews she had never met.

“Who made the map?”

“I did.”

“How did you know all those things?”

“Some I remembered. Some Father wrote in his letters. Others I learned when I returned to the city.”

“You returned?”

“Last month. For the first time. I went to the house, but it was gone. I went to the garden. I found the place where we buried the button.”

“The button was in the cottage.”

“That was from my coat. I left it with the note so you’d know it was me. The buried button was still beneath the rosebush. I put it back.”

Clara thought of the blue crosses scattered across the map.

“Why not simply come into the office?”

Daniel gave a faint, embarrassed smile. For an instant, she saw the boy who had once declared a button treasure.

“I was afraid.”

“You are seventy.”

“Fear ages well.”

Despite herself, Clara laughed.

It was not forgiveness. It was only laughter, small and cracked, but it opened a little space in the room.

Daniel walked her through the orchard before the afternoon train. He showed her the pear trees he had planted with Ruth, the shed he had built, the hill where his children once went sledding.

At the gate, he handed her a paper bag filled with late pears.

“Will you come again?” he asked.

Clara considered him.

“I have twenty-seven years of unused holiday,” she said. “I may come on Thursday.”

Daniel nodded, trying not to look relieved.

“And you will come to the city,” she added. “You will visit Mother’s grave.”

“Yes.”

“You will tell her yourself.”

“Yes.”

Clara walked back toward Bellweather station. Halfway down the lane, she unfolded the map.

She had assumed it recorded the past, but now she noticed a final blue cross on the reverse side. It marked the station beneath Platform Nine.

Beside it, Daniel had written:

**Where Clara decides what may be found.**

On Thursday, he arrived carrying the old silver button.

Clara met him beneath the station clock. They stood among travelers rushing toward arrivals and departures, each person holding tightly to what they had remembered to keep.

Daniel looked older than he had in the orchard. Or perhaps the station made everyone look temporary.

Together they went to the cemetery.

Afterward, Clara took him to the Lost Property Office. She showed him the endless shelves and the ledger containing thousands of abandoned things.

“Do people ever come back after many years?” he asked.

“Sometimes.”

“And do they get their belongings?”

“If they can describe them.”

Clara opened Drawer C and removed the hand-drawn map.

“Describe this,” she said.

Daniel looked puzzled, but he began.

“One sheet of paper. The city in pencil. Blue crosses. Folded twice.”

“Distinguishing marks?”

He met her eyes.

“A place where a silver button was buried. A place where a boy waited. A house with three pears.”

Clara consulted the ledger, though she knew the entry by heart.

“Name?”

He hesitated.

“Daniel Vale.”

She crossed out **Item 4,823** and wrote **CLAIMED** beside it.

Then she gave him the map.

They had lunch in the station café. Conversation came unevenly. They spoke of harmless things at first: trains, weather, pears, the price of tea. Later, they spoke of Ruth, Clara’s husband, their mother’s final years, and the childhood each had carried alone.

There were silences. Some were angry. Some were sad. A few were almost peaceful.

When Daniel’s train was announced, Clara walked him to the platform.

“Thursday?” he asked.

“Thursday,” she agreed.

He boarded and found a seat by the window. As the train began to move, he lifted one hand.

Clara lifted hers.

She remained on the platform until the final carriage disappeared beneath the iron roof.

Then she returned to the office.

That evening, while cataloguing a collection of items from the westbound trains, Clara found a child’s mitten, a brass compass, and a small wooden box with no lock.

Inside the box lay a single silver button engraved with an anchor.

For one impossible moment, she thought Daniel had left it behind again.

Then she noticed a folded scrap of paper beneath it.

**Treasure,** Daniel had written. **We’re the only ones who know where it is.**

Clara smiled.

She did not enter the box in the ledger. She placed it in her coat pocket and finished her work.

At six, she locked the cabinets, turned off the yellow lamps, and climbed the stairs to the station.

Outside, the city glittered after rain. Streets opened in every direction. Clara had spent most of her life believing that departures were singular events: a train leaving, a door closing, a boy failing to come home.

Now she understood that people departed by degrees. They left through fear, silence, pride, and passing years. Sometimes they traveled so far that no map could return them to the place they had begun.

But maps were not only for returning.

They were also for finding another road.

Clara put her hand in her pocket and touched the silver button. Then she crossed the station square, carrying the small, stubborn weight of what had been lost—and what, though altered beyond recognition, had finally been found.
